doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Missing the trumpet and coming back through Michael Gribrock
summary: He never liked guitar as much; Gribrock persuaded him to try trumpet again, and his brother's sub job started his New York career.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Playing guitar. And so I was starting to make a meager existence playing music. But the one thing that I realized was that — I kept on thinking well if I get the chops together I’ll start enjoying it as much as trumpet. Well I started developing technique and I got so that I could play it okay. But I never liked it as much. And it was only at the time when I started to get kind of a little bit proficient that I realized that there are some things that always bothered me about the guitar after playing the trumpet, one of which is that the sound is coming out of another place. It’s coming out of this amp over here. I could never get used to that. You know you’re playing here — a trumpet is just like an extension of your head, it feels like part of your body. Guitar always felt, with the electronics and everything, and to control your sound by turning dials and all that, I just could never — and not to mention hauling the amp around I mean I hated that. So about that time an old friend of mine from Indiana University just wanted to come to New York and we had an extra room in the apartment that we had that I was sharing with some other musicians. And so he came in and he knew me from when I was a trumpet player. And he said to me, “if you don’t want to play that’s one thing, but if you think it’s because of some physical thing, I really think that there’s a way to get around it and you should at least try.” His name is Michael Gribrock. And he’s still a really good friend of mine. And he talked me into just — here was a trumpet player who had had a lot of problems and stayed in Indiana, stuck it out studying and kind of managed to get over some of these things. And so the horn was there and I started to play it. And I realized immediately that whether I could play it well or just do it as a hobby, immediately I just enjoyed it much more. And it’s obvious that’s what it’s all about. So I thought all right, what the hell, I’ll just see what happens. And then shortly after I started studying with Vince Penzarella, about six months later my brother moved to town and there was a job he couldn’t make and so he said, “could you sub for me?” And so I ended up six months later I was working in New York, with no expectations of it being a career or anything. But it just kind of evolved.
That first time after, picking up the trumpet after ten years, did your chops remember what it felt like? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well yeah kind of, although I was conscious that I wanted to play differently than I had before because if I was going to do this I didn’t want to have the same problem. My fingers, when Mike was teaching me in the beginning said, “I’m used to teaching beginners who don’t know the fingerings, and here, it’s like —.” So I tried to play. I wasn’t trying to play high, loud, anything. But I would just play tunes, middle register things, and I really from the start felt that connection again.
